passage:
On Tuesday morning, in her rented flat in Mumbai, Aparna looked at her calendar and felt her stomach drop. She had promised Hrithik she would build the website for his tiffin service by Friday. Her office had just moved her project deadline to Thursday.
She could keep quiet and hope, or send a vague "something came up" on Friday night. Instead she called him before nine.
"Hrithik, I can't finish the full site by Friday. I'm sorry; I know you planned the launch around it." He was quiet. "What I can do: the home page and menu by Friday, so you can launch, and the order form by next Wednesday. If that doesn't work, I'll connect you with someone I know who freelances."
After a pause he said, "Home page is enough to launch. Thanks for telling me now."

qa.q: What had Aparna promised to build for Hrithik?
qa.a: She had promised to build the website for his tiffin service by Friday.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when she looked at her calendar, and why?
qa.a: She felt anxious, her stomach dropping, because the new office deadline meant she couldn't keep her promise to Hrithik.

qa.q: Which parts of Aparna's call made the change of plan work?
qa.a: She called early, owned the impact on his launch, and offered a clear smaller promise plus a backup, instead of vanishing or making vague excuses.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt if the message had come on Friday night instead?
qa.a: He would likely have felt let down and stuck, with his launch planned and no time to find another option.

grounding: When a promise can no longer be kept, a young woman says so early, owns the impact and offers what she truly can do.

passage:
"Before you pay the deposit," Charu said, twisting her dupatta, "I have to tell you something."
Kalyani put down her cup. "That sounds bad."
"I promised we'd take the two-bedroom together in June. I've got a job offer in another city, and I'm going to take it."
"Charu. We shortlisted that flat because of you."
"I know. That's why I'm telling you today and not in May. I've messed up your plan, and I'm sorry."
Kalyani stared out of the window. "So now what? I can't afford it alone."
"I've asked two colleagues who are looking for a room. One wants to see it on Saturday. And I'll pay my half of the token amount we already gave, even though I won't live there."
Kalyani let out a long breath. "Okay. Saturday. I'm still annoyed."
"That's fair."

qa.q: When does one of the colleagues want to see the flat?
qa.a: One of them wants to see it on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Kalyani feel after hearing Charu's news, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kalyani feels upset and worried; she stares out of the window, says she can't afford it alone, and admits she is still annoyed.

qa.q: Which choices made Charu's change of plan honest rather than a disappearance?
qa.a: Charu spoke before the deposit, admitted she had messed up the plan, and offered real help: finding colleagues and paying her half of the token amount.

qa.q: Why might Kalyani's trust in Charu survive this?
qa.a: Because Charu told her early and took responsibility, Kalyani can be annoyed without feeling betrayed.

grounding: A young woman who can no longer keep a promise to share a flat says so early, owns the impact and offers what she really can.
